title: First Day Where You Have Been in All the Rooms
statement:
There are `n` rooms numbered `0` to `n - 1`, and you are in exactly one room each day; days are numbered from `0`, and on day `0` you are in room `0`. Where you go next depends on the room `i` you are in today and on how many times you have now been in it, counting today:

- an **odd** count sends you tomorrow to room `nextVisit[i]`, which is never larger than `i`;
- an **even** count sends you tomorrow to room `(i + 1) mod n`.

Return the number of the first day by which every room has been entered at least once. Such a day always exists. The number can be huge, so return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating day by day is correct but hopeless: with every `nextVisit[i] = 0` the answer is `2^n - 2`. The useful fact is that you can only step from room `i` into room `i + 1` on an even visit, so at the moment you first enter room `i`, every lower room has an even count. Only parities matter for the rules, so the walk is fully determined by where you are.

Let `dp[i]` be the day you first enter room `i`. That visit is odd, so tomorrow you jump to `back = nextVisit[i]`. Now every room from `back` to `i - 1` has an even count again, exactly as when you first arrived at `back`, so walking back up to `i` repeats the same `dp[i] - dp[back]` days. Your second visit to `i` is even, and the next day you enter `i + 1`.

## Approach

1. Set `dp[0] = 0`: day 0 is spent in room 0.
2. For each `i` from `0` to `n - 2`, read `back = nextVisit[i]`.
3. `loop = dp[i] - dp[back]` is the length of the return walk; add `MOD` before `%` so it stays non-negative.
4. `dp[i + 1] = dp[i] + loop + 2`: one day to jump back, `loop` days to return, one day to step forward.
5. Rooms are first entered in increasing order, so return `dp[n - 1]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nextVisit = [0, 0]`, so `dp = [0, 0]`. For `i = 0`: `back = 0`, `loop = 0 - 0 = 0`, and `dp[1] = 0 + 0 + 2 = 2`. The answer is `dp[1] = 2`: room 0 on days 0 and 1, room 1 on day 2.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one constant-time update per room.
- Space: O(n) for `dp`.

## Pitfalls

- After reducing modulo `MOD`, `dp[i]` can be smaller than `dp[back]`; subtracting without adding `MOD` gives a negative result.
- Simulation times out: the day count can double with each room.
- When `nextVisit[i] === i`, `loop` is 0 and the room costs exactly two days; no special case is needed.
- `nextVisit[n - 1]` never affects the answer, because the count stops at the first entry into the last room.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | the modulus `10^9 + 7` |
| `n` | number of rooms |
| `dp[i]` | first day you enter room `i`, modulo `MOD` |
| `i` | the room whose first entry is known |
| `back` | the room an odd visit to `i` sends you to |
| `loop` | days needed to walk from `back` up to `i` again |

narration.4: dp[i] will hold the first day room i is entered; dp[0] is day 0.
narration.6: Use the first entry into room i to work out the first entry into room i + 1.
narration.7: The first visit to room i is odd, so tomorrow you are sent back to this room.
narration.8: Walking from back up to i again repeats the same days it took the first time; add MOD so the difference is not negative.
narration.9: One day to jump back, loop days to return, and one more day to step into room i + 1.
narration.11: Rooms are first entered in order, so the last room's first day is the answer.
